summary: A 1976 paper describing a distributed capability computing system, where access to resources is controlled by unforgeable tokens called capabilities. It was prepared for a conference and is shared as a preprint.

eli5.summary: Instead of passwords, you carry keys that cannot be copied. This paper describes sharing computers across a network that way.

subtitle: A distributed system using capabilities to control access across networks

tldr.problem: Distributed systems need a way to grant and verify access to resources across network boundaries. Traditional password-based authentication can reveal credentials during transmission, and each system may use a different access control model.
tldr.mechanism: The Distributed Capability Computing System (DCCS) extends capability-based access control across networks. Capabilities are unforgeable tokens that grant rights to invoke a specific service. A process uses a capability from its capability list to invoke a service; the service can be local, remote, or emulated.
tldr.outcome: The capability model proved influential in security research and operating system design, though widespread deployment of DCCS did not occur. Capability-based security remains a significant conceptual framework.

today: RFC 712 is a foundational design for capability-based distributed computing. Although the specific DCCS was not widely deployed, the capability model remains influential in security research and influenced subsequent operating system designs and language-based security.

sections.title: Capability-Based Access Control
sections.content:
RFC 712 describes a distributed computing system built on capability-based access control. In a traditional system, processes send requests to a system call interface. In a capability system, a process holds a list of capabilities—protected references to objects it is allowed to use. All system requests are actually invocations on capabilities in the process's list. A capability cannot be forged or copied; the system protects it.

The key advantage is that access rights are unforgeable. To grant permission to a resource, you pass a capability; no password is transmitted, and the recipient cannot create fake capabilities. The system maintains this guarantee even when capabilities are passed across a network.
sections.eli5: A capability is like a signed ticket. You show it to use something, and nobody can fake one. When you give your ticket to someone else, they can use it the same way you could, but they cannot make up their own ticket.

sections.title: Emulation and Network Protocol
sections.content:
The DCCS extends capability systems to networks by allowing one process to emulate a remote capability. When a local process invokes a capability that points to a remote host, the local host sends an invoke message over the network to the remote host. The remote host invokes the actual capability and returns the result. To the invoking process, the emulated capability behaves exactly like the real capability, except for network delays.

If an invocation returns a capability, the supporting host allocates a new slot in its capability list and returns a descriptor identifying the remote host and the slot number. The emulating host creates a new requestor (a capability created by a server) with that descriptor, so the returned capability can be invoked by the original process.
sections.eli5: Your local computer can pretend to have a key to a distant resource. When you use it, your computer asks the distant computer to actually use the key and sends back the result. If the distant key unlocks something new, your computer gets a new key that works the same way.

sections.title: Capabilities and Network Messages
sections.content:
The DCCS defines primitive capabilities for different purposes: File (read and write data), Directory (manage collections of other capabilities), Process (access process memory and capability lists), and Server (implement new capability types). Each invocation passes data and capabilities as parameters; the parameter descriptor specifies how many bits and capabilities are passed and returned.

Timing is critical: because invocations can take a long time, the emulating process queues requests and continues servicing other invocations. The supporting host similarly spawns a separate process to invoke the actual capability, so network requests are not blocked. The protocol maintains multiple outstanding requests between hosts using request identifiers.
sections.eli5: When you use a capability, you can pass information and other keys as arguments. The system tells both ends how much is coming and how much to expect back. Because some operations take a long time, the program does not stop waiting—it can do other things.
